lignes.texte: Canada has just walked into a vicious economic trap.
For 80 years, the relationship between the U.S. and Canada seemed unbreakable. Now, tensions are
brewing and trade talks have collapsed. A brutal volley of tariffs has forced Prime Minister Mark
Carney to draw a line in the sand. Canada will not be held hostage.
Military and trade ties have been completely severed. But there’s one problem. Every pipeline,
trainline and shipping route points south. Canada wanted economic independence. Instead, they
gave America the kill switch. And the worst part? Washington hasn’t even retaliated… yet.
Living next door to the most powerful military and economy on Earth, meant Canada reaped
staggering benefits. Geography made most of that wealth possible. But it also created
something far more complicated: A dangerous structural illusion.
By 2025, the U.S. accounted for over three-quarters of Canadian exports of goods,
while supplying almost half of its imports. It’s worth over $900 billion, making it the largest
bilateral trading relationship in the world. Every single year Canada has pumped tens of
billions of dollars into the U.S. through heavy hitters like precious metals,
vehicles and nuclear reactors. But away from the headlines, obscure items like wigs, egg-grading
equipment, and dog muzzles have steadily flowed south into vast, lucrative markets.
And America reciprocates. Billions of dollars’ worth machinery,
electronics and plastics move north. There’s also millions of smaller items like pet food and fries.
Canada’s economy has become hardwired into the U.S. market. It relies on it to survive.it. And
that dependency is most critical in one sector. Energy.
In 2025, Canada exported 6.5 million barrels per day of hydrocarbons globally. The U.S. to
the bulk of that, taking a massive 90.8%. That supply makes up nearly two thirds of
all the crude oil and close to 100% of all the natural gas imported by the U.S.
Dozens of pipelines, power lines, and a web of rail and shipping corridors lock the countries
together. It’s a structural integration at a level that makes sudden decoupling almost
physically impossible. Or so you’d think.
Because Mark Carney just filed for economic divorce.
In late August 2026, after months of escalating tensions, trade talks collapsed. Both sides are
pointing the finger of blame at each other. Carney said that “[America] asked too much,
and they offered too little.” According to him, the U.S. pulled a
last minute bait and switch, introducing “unfair [and] uneconomic” terms. Canadian officials
claimed the U.S. had blocked heavy trucks from tariff relief, reneged on a deal to slash tariffs
on Canadian aluminum and steel. But that’s not all. They said the U.S. wanted to control
Canada’s steel tariffs with other countries, and even floated the idea of having a veto over
Canada’s future free-trade agreements. The U.S. sees things differently.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that Canada had backed out of terms
they had already “agreed earlier [in the] week”. He also added that Canada
has walked back on other commitments. Later, in an interview with CNBC, he put it more bluntly:
“They wanted more.” The rest of Washington fell into line.
Vice President JD Vance accused Canada of bringing “unreasonable last-minute demands”
and were trying to “take advantage of America.” By early September, Commerce Secretary Howard
Lutnick claimed Canada “blew up” a nearly complete deal “for political reasons.”
Behind the rhetoric, the U.S. has a massive list of complaints.
Canada banned U.S. alcohol in 8 out of 10 Canadian provinces. Auto tariffs that were lingering from
the original U.S./Canadian tariff war from 2025. And Canada’s notorious protected dairy policies.
Both sides had serious issues and concerns. Resolving them required skill, patience,
and actual diplomacy. Something that two long term allies could figure out, right?
Wrong. Washington detonated a grenade.
The administration slapped 50% tariffs on CAD$20 billion of exports, including wine, furniture,
dairy, cement, clothing and sporting goods. Even the Canadian wigs got hit, as well as “articles
for Christmas festivities,” and a host of other eclectic and often exotic products.
Carney hit straight back. Counter-tariffs of 15 to 50% were
applied to roughly $20 billion of U.S. goods and took effect just after midnight on September 8th.
Iron, steel, and aluminum products make up almost half of the list,
a direct mirror to the U.S. tariffs that started this economic death spiral. Canada is also
targeting other “big ticket” items like plastics, electrical machinery, furniture, and cosmetics.
Because the tit-for-tat tariffs are so far-reaching, they’re going to hammer
ordinary consumers and businesses of all sizes. Tariffs are inflationary. They act like a sponge,
absorbing the purchasing power right out of your money. But there
was something else lurking in the background. A shadow hanging over this entire trade war.
Carney wants to slash defense spending with America.
While it wasn’t publicly blamed for the breakdown of the August talks,
Canada's push to reduce its dependence on U.S. defense suppliers added serious
fuel to the fire. That single move threatens to tank the Canadian dollar,
and leave the country vulnerable. It all traces back to April 2026,
and the Liberal Party’s national convention. Mark Carney stood before delegates and declared:
“The days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the U.S. are over.”
It was a standing-ovation moment. While it was a fiery speech,
Carney was also outlining a radical transformation of Canadian defense policy.
According to the Prime Minister’s office, over 70% of Canada’s military capital
spending flows directly to U.S. suppliers. It’s been a structural reality for decades,
born out of geography, convenience, and the quality of U.S. military tech. But more
importantly, the implicit assumption that the U.S. would always be a reliable ally.
Carney was effectively declaring that assumption DOA.
But declaring independence and actually achieving it are two different things.
The new Defense Industrial Strategy unveiled by Carney aims to do something radical: award
70% of defense procurement contracts to domestic firms. It also sets ambitious long-term targets,
like boosting defense industry revenues by more than 240%, increasing defense exports by 50%,
and creating up to 125,000 jobs. It’s a bold vision for Canadian military sovereignty…
On paper. In reality, it’s a logistical nightmare.
Nearly half of everything Canada’s defense sector builds is shipped out of the country. 63% of
that went to the U.S., with small percentages going to the U.K., Australia, and New Zealand.
Canadian defense firms are deeply ingrained in U.S. supply chains.
In fact, many of the Canadian military exports are built by subsidiaries of U.S. companies.
Take the Stryker. The legendary armored vehicle is the backbone of the U.S. army.
But it’s based on a Canadian designed vehicle and made by General Dynamics Land Systems – Canada,
or GDLS-C… a wholly owned subsidiary of U.S. giant General Dynamics Corporation,
headquartered in Reston, Virginia. So the U.S.’s signature ground
vehicle is a Canadian design, built in Canada, by an American owned company.
There are similar dynamics at play across Canada’s other top exports,
including sensors and ammunition. The irony is that under Carney’s “Buy
Canadian” policy, these U.S.-owned subsidiaries are considered Canadian. A July 2026 report
exposed the truth. Foreign-owned companies scooped up more than 70% of the contracts
examined under the Buy Canadian policy. The entire policy is an illusion.
The “redirection” of money isn’t about where the profits end up, more where the invoice is written.
But while the finances are murky, the security nightmare facing Canada is clear.
Canada imports a wide range of military equipment from the U.S., some of it critical for the
nation’s security. Canada’s flagship $77 billion fleet of 15 River-class destroyers is currently
under construction. The hulls are British, but their entire combat system, including the
Aegis Combat System, and Tomahawk missiles, is U.S.-made. You can’t pull those systems without
completely redesigning the ship It’s functionally impossible.
Canada also has no viable alternatives to replace its U.S.-made strategic airlift aircraft.
Canada relies on its 5 C-17 Globemasters for its strategic airlift capability. The C-17 is the only
aircraft that can fly a 60-ton Leopard 2 over 1,000 miles (1,609 km). Building an equivalent
would be extremely expensive and time consuming. If it could be done at all.
Even more problematic would be the loss of U.S. GPS.
Canada has no sovereign positioning, navigation, or timing capability,
or PNT for short. Every vehicle, aircraft, and ship depends on the U.S.’s GPS constellation.
Europe’s Galileo exists, but it’s not a drop-in replacement for encrypted, military-grade American
GPS. Building a Canadian version would take 15 to 20 years and cost tens of billions of dollars.
Canada also has zero ballistic missile defense, or BMD. It relies entirely on Washington to intercept
any incoming threats.There is no Canadian backup and no domestic capacity to build one.
Slamming the door on U.S. defence isn’t as simple as building new factories. A whole
industrial ecosystem has to be created. While that happens, Canada is exposed.
That’s why Carney’s 70 cents defense declaration cast a toxic shadow over the recent trade talks.
It also likely contributed to their breakdown. Now, the trade war escalation that has followed
threatens to push the entire Canadian economy off a cliff.
In the first half of 2026, Canada shipped almost 68% of its total exports to the
U.S. It reinforced the reality that Canada’s export infrastructure is built for one market.
If the tariff war crushes Canadian competitiveness in America, companies will have to find new
markets immediately… or face economic ruin. But even if it finds customers in different
parts of the world, how exactly is it going to physically supply them?
The ports at Vancouver and Prince Rupert can’t handle even a fraction of the goods
that flow south. The pipelines can’t reroute overnight. The rail lines don’t
switch direction. And the integrated automotive supply chains can’t be untangled without years
of investment and massive disruption. Still, Carney has vowed to diversify
Canada’s trade away from the U.S. And on paper, he’s made a decent start.
By July 2026, the share of U.S.-bound Canadian exports had dropped to 66% from an average of
75 percent before the trade war. But that’s still a massive dependency. Doubling non-U.S. exports
over the next decade, requires infrastructure that doesn’t exist, trade agreements that haven’t been
signed, and customers who aren’t buying. And this is where the math gets brutal.
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs cover $20 billion of U.S. goods. But Canada is picking a fight against
an economy 13 times its size. That’s not a fair fight.
The North American auto industry is the poster child for cross-border supply chains. Or at
least it has been. Parts cross the border multiple times before a vehicle rolls off
the assembly line on one side or the other. But the Trump administration has threatened
to raise U.S. tariffs on all cars, trucks, and automotive parts from Canada to 50% starting
January 1st, 2027. It would be catastrophic for producers on both sides of the border,
not to mention consumers. Then, there’s energy.
Canada supplies 64% of all U.S. crude oil imports. While the U.S. desperately needs that energy,
Canada is trapped. The pipelines run south. The refineries are in the U.S. Midwest. And
the shipping capacity to export to Asia or Europe doesn’t exist at the scale required.
It’s impossible to just shut this all down and skip happily over to new markets. It
spells disaster for ordinary Canadians. They’ll be faced with job losses, supply chain disruptions,
reduced competitiveness, and higher prices. It’s going to be painful.
So when Carney talks about cutting the 70-cent defense dollar, he’s not just
making a geopolitical statement. He’s committing to a decade or more of economic hurt in exchange
for long-term sovereignty. The question is whether
Canada can survive the transition. To be fair, his instinct is understandable.
His tough stance with Donald Trump seems to have the support of the majority of Canadians,
despite the high potential for disaster. Polls in the days immediately after reciprocal tariffs
were announced showed anywhere from 63 to 85% support for his actions.
The Carney government was forged in the shadow of a trade war and threats
of annexation from President Trump. While the U.S. House voted to reject certain tariffs,
the President maintained a hardline stance, using emergency economic powers to justify duties on
Canadian autos, steel, and aluminum. Now, trust in Washington has eroded.
That seemingly unshakeable alliance has been battered. And it's not
just Canada reassessing its options. Alistair Edgar, an associate professor of
political science at Wilfrid Laurier University, sees this as a “fundamental rupture”. In his
words, “The U.S. can no longer be considered a reliable and trusted ally and partner,”
Erika Simpson, an associate professor of international relations at Western University,
offers a more measured view. According to her, Canada’s plan reflects a cautious strategic
adjustment rather than a decisive break. “This should be understood as recalibration
rather than rupture,” Simpson said. But even she acknowledges the difficult situation Canada is in.
Economically and militarily, it is more or less joined at the hip to its southern neighbor. Any
decoupling will of necessity have to be gradual. And that’s the problem.
Carney’s rhetoric promises radical change. But in reality it’s going to be a slow, painful,
uncertain transition. For both countries. Which begs the question: When a middle power
cuts off its only superpower customer, which side runs out of money first?
Despite its much smaller size, Canada does have some leverage. The U.S. needs Canadian energy,
and Canadian minerals are critical for the U.S.’s defense industry. The integrated supply
chains would take years to untangle. And the pain would ripple across on both sides of the border.
But Canada is the smaller economy and therefore the one with more to lose. It's the one that will
have to build enormous domestic capacity in sectors that have been neglected for decades.
Carney’s vision of “Buy Canadian” steel, aluminum, lumber, and workers is politically
powerful. But it’s also economically fraught. It’s an inspiring goal. The question is whether
Canada has the time, the capital, and the resilience to achieve it before the
costs of decoupling break the country. Carney continues to enjoy broad support
from Canadians. But political analysts warn that support could disappear as
the consequences of the trade war sink in. That’s why the Canadian Chamber of Commerce
has urged the Carney government to take a surgical approach to retaliation. “Businesses understand
retaliation but don’t want to see endless escalation,” said CEO and President Candace Laing.
But endless escalation is what’s happening. Tariffs upon tariffs. Threats of further
tariffs. A trade war that has already lasted 18 months and shows no sign of ending. And
underneath it all, the beginnings of the U.S. defense dominance cracking.
The collapse of American defense hegemony won’t happen in a single,
sudden event. The U.S. military has been too powerful for too long, and too deeply embedded
globally to just disappear overnight. It’ll be a grinding realignment driven
by forces that no single leader can control. It’s happening in Europe. The EU is steering
military budgets towards European weapons systems, instead of American hardware.
Gulf States are realizing the U.S. can’t protect them from Iranian missiles the way they thought.
And it’s being seen in Carney’s tough stance. His 70 cents declaration is a symptom of that
slow collapse, not the cause. It’s a political response to a geopolitical
reality. From Canada’s perspective, the U.S. is no longer a reliable ally and Canada must adapt.
But that takes time. And time is the one resource Canada doesn’t have.
The integrated supply chains, the shared infrastructure, the decades of economic
interdependence can’t be unwound with a rousing speech. The applause in Montreal will fade. But
the factories in Ontario and Quebec will still need parts. The pipelines will still flow south,
even if they’re empty. And the auto plants will still stop production
when tariffs make them unsustainable. Canada is trapped by its own declaration
of independence. And the only way out is through years of economic suffering,
strategic uncertainty, and difficult choices. The days of 70 cents of every dollar to the
U.S. are over. A new geopolitical reality is dawning. And no one knows how this ends.
But by the looks of things, it’s not going to end well.
